# GateKit Map

> Three maps of Baldur's Gate 3, built by [GateKit](https://github.com/bg3gk/gatekit) and served
> by the engine in [bg3gk/map](https://github.com/bg3gk/map): the game's own content read out of
> an ordinary installation, our map of the engine's ECS components, and facts about the engine's
> binaries. No API key; a page and its data are one thing.
> Built from {{SOURCE}}.

## The rule

Every object has a URL. Add `.json` to it and you get the page as data - and the `.json` is all
there is: a browser that opens the address is served a shell that fetches the same file and
draws it, so what a person reads and what you fetch cannot differ. Fetch the `.json` directly.
Build the address from an id you already have; there is nothing to scrape.

```
{{BASE}}entity/<uuid>          a character or an item placed in a level
{{BASE}}dialog/<name>          a dialogue, by its name without the folder it is filed in
{{BASE}}timeline/<uuid>        the staging of a dialogue
{{BASE}}template/<uuid>        a root template
{{BASE}}stat/<name>            one named row of the game's stat files
{{BASE}}level/<name>           a level, and what it places
{{BASE}}loca/<handle>          a line of the game's text, in every language
{{BASE}}object/<key>           an object as the game's file declares it, with every attribute
{{BASE}}source/<package>/<path> a file the index read, and every object it declares
{{BASE}}package/<name>         a package of the game, and every file inside it
{{BASE}}osiris/<name>          a name of the story scripts, and every script that uses it
{{BASE}}component/<name>       an engine component, what its memory holds and where it was seen
{{BASE}}symbol/<name>          a class of the engine, its declared layout and its exported methods
{{BASE}}enum/<name>            an enumeration of the engine
{{BASE}}function/<binary>+0x<rva>  a function of the engine's binaries: bg3.exe, bg3_dx11.exe or a Toolkit DLL
```

A C++ name is qualified with `::`, which is not a usable path segment everywhere, so a dot
stands in for it: `ecl::ActiveTurnComponent` is at `{{BASE}}component/ecl.ActiveTurnComponent`.
Anything else outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` is written as `!` and two hex digits of its UTF-8
bytes - `Background_LegendOfBaldur'sGate` is `stat/Background_LegendOfBaldur!27sGate` - and is
asked for exactly as written. Two ids that differ only in case get `~2`, `~3` appended to the
later one in ordinal order.

What this site holds: {{COUNTS}}.

## Searching

`{{BASE}}api/search?q=<words>` answers JSON:

```json
{
  "exact": "dialog/...",
  "pages": [ { "kind": "...", "route": "...", "name": "...", "note": "..." } ],
  "lines": [ { "handle": "h...", "lang": "English", "text": "... <em>word</em> ..." } ],
  "names": [ { "name": "...", "node": "...", "key": "...", "route": "..." } ]
}
```

`exact` is set when what you asked is the id of exactly one page; the lists are then empty.
Every word is matched by its beginning, all of them must match, and `&lang=<language>` keeps the
lines to one language. Lines of Chinese, Japanese and Korean are matched anywhere in the line,
three characters or more. `names` are objects of the game found by name; `route` is set on those
that have a page. A search is limited per address per minute; an answer of `429` says to wait.

An address is found the way a decompiler shows it, too: `bg3.exe+0x77F580`, `0x14077F580` or
`FUN_14077f580` answers with the function it is in - and for an absolute address, with the
function in each build of the game, because both are loaded at the same base. The absolute
addresses assume each binary's default base: `0x140000000` for an executable, `0x180000000` for a
library.

An object whose key is given twice has two pages, the second at `object/<key>.<row>`; an object
with no key is at `object/row.<row>`.

Languages: {{LANGUAGES}}.

## The shape of the JSON

```json
{
  "kind": "dialog", "id": "...", "route": "dialog/...",
  "title": "...", "subtitle": "...",
  "fields":   { "timeline": <value>, "nodes": <value>, ... },
  "sections": [ { "title": "Lines", "columns": [...], "shown": 200, "total": 1430,
                  "rows": [ [ <value>, ... ] ] } ],
  "hints":    { "<a field or column name>": "what it means" },
  "links":    [ <value>, ... ],
  "index":    { "origin": "game", "fullIndex": "map fetch", "about": "{{BASE}}llms.txt" }
}
```

Every `route`, at the top of a page or inside a value, is relative to the site root: the URL is
`{{BASE}}` plus the route. Field names are unique on a page and are written in the order the page
shows them.

A `<value>` is written as small as it can be said:

| what you get | what it is |
|---|---|
| `null` | nothing at all |
| `"some text"` | ordinary prose |
| `12.5` | a number |
| `{"route": "template/<uuid>"}` | **a link**: the kind is the first segment, the id is the rest |
| `{"id": "VFX_Blood"}` | names something that has no page here |
| `{"path": "Public/Shared/Stats/…"}` | a file path inside the game's packages |

`"text"` appears on a link only when what is shown differs from the last segment of the route
read back - every `!xx` as a byte of UTF-8. Any of the object forms may carry `"note"`, a few
words saying what the identifier is. A link to a line of text carries the line itself: in
English as its `note` (or its `text`, where the line is what the table is about), and in every
other language in `"texts": {"<language>": "..."}` - so resolving a line costs no second request.

`links` is every distinct object the page names, in the order it appears. Follow those and you
have walked the web.

`index.origin` says whose material a page is: `game` for Larian's text, published under the
promise below, and `ours` for what we measured - the component map, the classes and the
enumerations. A section whose `total` is larger than its `shown` was cut; the rest are in the
databases `map fetch` downloads.

## The thread between the three maps

It runs both ways:

- a **component** page lists where it was seen - each sighting names a **dialogue** or an
  **object**, and links to it;
- an **object** page lists the components seen on it, the **template** it was made from, the
  **level** it is placed in and the **dialogues** it speaks in;
- a **dialogue** page lists the components seen while it played, its lines, and the
  **timelines** that stage it;
- a **line** of text lists every language, the recordings that voice it and where it is said;
- a **timeline** page lists its actors and the tracks that hide or show a piece of gear;
- a **level** page lists what it places and the components seen while it was loaded;
- a **component** page names the **class** it is, which has its own page among the symbols, and
  a **symbol** page names our map of it, if we have mapped it.

## When something fails

A page that cannot be drawn says so on a red d20 that has landed on a 1 - a critical failure -
with the reason underneath. The reason names the HTTP status where the server answered with one,
and otherwise ends with one of these numbers:

| code | what failed |
|---|---|
| `1` | the site could not be reached: the connection or the server is down |
| `2` | the search could not be answered |
| `4` | the data of a page could not be read |

An address with no page is not a failure: it answers 404 with the shell, which says there is no
such page and shows what the search finds for it.

## What is not here

- Art, audio, video, fonts and textures. The index records that a resource exists and what it is
  called; it never carries the resource.
- The engine's code. Names, addresses, sizes, layouts and calls are facts about it and are here;
  decompiled code is not, and never will be.

## The promise

The game's content here is Larian Studios'. <https://github.com/bg3gk/map#readme> says how to
ask for it to be taken down.

The component map and the facts about the engine's binaries are ours: they are the result of
reading and measuring a running game, and no file of the game contains them.

The site is kept out of search engines: every answer says `noindex`, and `robots.txt` lets
crawlers read this file and nothing else. A copy of the game's text in someone else's index
would outlive the day it was withdrawn here. An agent fetching a page because a person asked
it to is not a crawler, and is welcome.
